metadata.title: TMUA 2023 · Paper 1
metadata.description: Worked steps, progressive hints and reviewed follow-up questions.

matches.rationale: Both integrate expressions with unknown constants, translate integral and value conditions into simultaneous linear equations, and eliminate the constants. The candidate first reconstructs a quadratic from its second derivative.

Both impose a strictly negative discriminant on a monic parameter-dependent quadratic and solve a strict parameter interval. The candidate starts from positivity for all inputs instead of a no-intersection statement.

Both equate a line and a quadratic curve, compute the resulting discriminant and solve its parameter condition. The candidate includes tangency and crossing, so equality must be retained instead of excluded.
Both combine signed definite integrals using adjacent intervals and linear relations without finding an antiderivative. The candidate also translates an input shift into shifted bounds.

Both assign subinterval integrals, use additivity to solve overlapping integral information, and combine the signed contributions. The candidate additionally turns the signed lobes into total geometric area.

Both use exact sine values under repeated angle shifts to group a trigonometric series. The candidate practises the periodic-sign grouping prerequisite through finite cancellation; it does not use the original geometric denominator or infinite-sum formula.

Both identify a GP first term and signed ratio, verify convergence and evaluate an infinite sum. The candidate practises that GP operation from given terms; it does not derive the ratio from a trigonometric numerator.

Both decide integrality or divisibility by checking prime exponents separately. The candidate practises that prime-factor prerequisite; the original additionally derives binomial coefficients and counts their indices.

Both rewrite related powers using a positive exponential variable, solve its quadratic and recover valid original inputs. The candidate has nested outer powers and excludes zero; the original adds the ratio equation and asks for the larger input.

Both use a positive exponential substitution to expose a quadratic, retain permitted roots and use exponential monotonicity when recovering ordered original inputs. The candidate combines the two inputs as a logarithmic difference instead of selecting the larger.

Both retain two SSA triangles, use the cosine rule on their unknown third sides, and relate their areas through a common fixed side and angle. The candidate uses a supplied area ratio to recover a cosine instead of computing the ratio.

Both must retain the two nondegenerate SSA configurations for one angle and two sides. The candidate derives the strict altitude-side inequalities guaranteeing both triangles, rather than using their two roots to calculate an area ratio.

Both recover the possible signed cosine levels from a squared equation and count all intersections over an interval with a scaled angular input. The candidate first infers the allowed level range from an earlier root count.

Both reduce an algebraic trigonometric equation to permissible levels, scale the complete angular interval and enumerate its solutions including endpoints. The candidate uses a sine quadratic and asks for the largest input rather than a count.

Both compare a trapezium approximation with the signed exact integral. The candidate isolates the error-direction prerequisite under graph transformations; it does not calculate the original semicircle area or strip-height sum.

Both complete a quadratic square to locate a vertex, then follow how parameter changes alter its coordinates. The candidate compares direction of movement; the original recovers a horizontal scale from a translated vertex.

Both track horizontal input scaling and translations in a quadratic, using the transformed vertex to check the formula. The candidate supplies a sequence of transformations to execute, whereas the original asks for the scale parameter.

Both express a trigonometric equation as a polynomial in a squared trigonometric quantity, filter its allowed range and count every angular solution in a closed interval. The original additionally equates exponential powers and excludes tangent poles.

Both solve a polynomial condition in a restricted trigonometric quantity, recover all permitted sine or cosine signs and enumerate the original angles. The candidate uses absolute cosine rather than tangent and an exponential comparison.

Both read circle centres and radii, compute centre separation and use collinear circle points to attain an extreme point-to-point distance. The candidate asks for the shortest disjoint gap, so radii are subtracted instead of added for the farthest points.

Both recover a centre from a circle equation and use coordinate distance from that centre. The candidate isolates the centre-distance prerequisite and identifies required parameters; it does not optimise separation of two moving boundary points.

Both differentiate a cubic, calculate its two turning heights and impose a positive local maximum and negative local minimum for three distinct roots. The candidate uses a single vertical parameter instead of two.

Both decide cubic root counts from the signs of the two stationary heights and treat repeated-root boundaries separately. The candidate then tests a sufficient condition for one root instead of the original exact interval for three roots.

Both pass the attained sine or cosine interval through a positive exponential and use the restricted output range to locate an extremum. The candidate then optimises a quadratic in that exponential; it does not solve the original reciprocal-base separation equation.

Both compute finite perpendicular gradients from coordinate data and use the resulting line conditions to determine unknown geometry. The candidate practises that perpendicular-line prerequisite with an area calculation; it does not require the original exhaustive choice of the right-angle vertex.

Both use perpendicular gradients to constrain unknown coordinate differences and verify a right-angled geometric figure. The candidate isolates this step using a rectangle and adds a side-length area calculation; it does not enumerate three possible right-angle vertices.

Both normalise a circle equation and complete the coordinate squares to find its radius. The candidate isolates the circle-radius prerequisite; it does not sum alternate nested-circle bands or an arithmetic progression.

Both use the convergence condition and infinite geometric-sum formula with symbolic parameters. The candidate practises solving GP parameter conditions and powered-term sums; the original instead filters a random integer parameter by an inequality.
Both check convergent GP ratios and evaluate infinite sums. The candidate recovers two ratios from term information; it does not perform the original strict threshold or finite probability count.

Both resolve an absolute value separately on the negative and nonnegative input regions before integrating polynomial pieces. The candidate computes a definite signed integral; the original joins the primitives and checks differentiability at zero.

Both replace the output of an inner function by a variable, complete the outer quadratic square and check whether its extremising input belongs to the attained inner range. The candidate uses an exponential positive range and requests only the minimum.

Both use an attained inner range and a quadratic vertex to establish an extreme. The candidate first minimises a positive quadratic denominator and then takes its reciprocal; it does not compare both endpoints of the original bounded interval.
